recipes.title: How to Make Fresh Tomato Sauce
recipes.source_note: Cooking Light Magazine March 2009 - Cooking Class
recipes.description: Fresh tomato sauce is a staple in Italy, where it's usually served with spaghetti. Although the sauce tastes rich and delicious, it only takes about 30 minutes to prepare. See recipe on page 138.

instructions.text: To peel tomatoes, core and cut a small X through the skin on the bottom of tomatoes with a sharp knife. Place them in boiling water for about 30 seconds or just until skins begin to peel back. Quickly remove tomatoes from pan, and plunge them into ice water. Drain and remove skins. Cut each tomato in half lengthwise, and squeeze the juices and seeds into a colander over a bowl. Reserve tomato juices, and discard seeds. Finely chop tomatoes.
Heat extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add garlic, and cook just until it begins to brown lightly, taking care not to burn it.
Add tomatoes and reserved juices, and cook until almost all of the liquid evaporates.

Finish cooking the pasta with the sauce, which should be in a skillet large enough to combine the two and allow for tossing. Add enough of the pasta cooking water to the sauce to give the dish a creamy texture and marry the sauce to the pasta.

notes: To peel tomatoes, core and cut a small X through the skin on the bottom with a sharp knife. Place in boiling water for about 30 seconds or just until skins begin to peel back. Quickly remove and plunge into ice water.
Add garlic, and cook just until it begins to brown lightly, taking care not to burn it.
Add enough of the pasta cooking water to the sauce to give the dish a creamy texture and marry the sauce to the pasta.
Learn about common pasta shapes and how to pair them with the proper sauce at CookingLight.com/features

recipes.title: How to Make Fresh Pasta
recipes.source_note: Cooking Light Magazine March 2009 - Cooking Class
recipes.description: In Emilia-Romagna, the region in Italy where fresh pasta rules, the dough is classically made with soft wheat flour and whole fresh eggs. Purists in the province prefer pasta doughs that have been rolled out on a wooden board to those rolled out with a machine, saying that sauce clings much better to the hand-rolled variety.

instructions.text: Place flour, salt, and eggs in a food processor, and process until combined and crumbly—the mixture won't form a ball.
Transfer to a lightly floured surface, and knead several minutes to form a soft dough. Then wrap dough into a disc, wrap it tightly with plastic, and allow it to rest for at least 20 minutes.

Divide dough into equal portions. Pass each portion through rollers with width gauge on the widest setting to stretch pasta. Run dough through rollers in each successive setting, moving gauge to a lower setting after each pass to form pasta sheets.

notes: For ravioli: Lay one pasta sheet on a flat, lightly floured work surface. Spoon the filling at three-inch intervals along the length of the sheet, leaving plenty of space on all sides.
Use a pastry brush or your fingers to moisten the edges, and the space between the filling portions on each pasta sheet, with water. Place a second pasta sheet over filling, pressing edges to seal.

assumptions: Serving size inferred from basics category

recipes.title: Classic Pasta Dough
recipes.source_note: Cooking Light Magazine March 2009 - Cooking Class
recipes.description: Italians use soft wheat flour to make fresh pasta. We tested the recipe with soft wheat flour and all-purpose flour and tasted them side by side, and we much prefer the soft wheat version—it gives the pasta a silkier texture. Order Italian-style flour from www.kingarthurflour.com, or look for Italian 00 flour at gourmet or online stores. Use this dough to make Ravioli with Herbed Ricotta Filling (page 141).

instructions.text: Weigh or lightly spoon flour into dry measuring cups; level with a knife. Combine flour, salt, and eggs in a food processor; pulse 10 times or until mixture is crumbly (dough will not form a ball). Turn dough out onto a lightly floured surface; knead until smooth and elastic (about 4 minutes). Shape dough into a disc; wrap with plastic wrap. Let dough stand at room temperature for 20 minutes.

Unwrap dough. Divide dough into 8 equal portions. Working with 1 portion at a time (keep remaining dough covered to prevent drying), pass dough through pasta rollers of a pasta machine on the widest setting. Fold dough in half crosswise; fold in half again. Pass dough through rollers again. Move width gauge to next setting; pass pasta through rollers. Continue moving width gauge to narrower settings; pass dough through rollers once at each setting to form 8 (15 x 3-inch) pasta strips. Lay strips flat on a lightly floured surface; cover. Repeat procedure with remaining dough portions. Yield: 4 servings (serving size: 2 ounces uncooked pasta).

notes: CALORIES 178; FAT 2.9g (sat 0.8g, mono 1g, poly 0.3g); PROTEIN 6.9g; CARB 30.2g; FIBER 0.2g; CHOL 106mg; IRON 0.9mg; SODIUM 107mg; CALC 21mg

recipes.title: Peppered Whipped Goat Cheese
recipes.description: Light, creamy whipped goat cheese seasoned with black pepper.

instructions.text: Using a hand mixer or fork, whip the goat cheese, cream, salt and pepper until light, creamy, and fluffy.

recipes.title: Butter-Toasted Almonds
recipes.description: Golden, aromatic sliced almonds toasted in butter.

instructions.text: Heat butter in a small sauté pan over medium-low heat.
Add almonds in a single layer. Cook 3-5 minutes, shaking pan frequently, until golden and aromatic.
Transfer to a bowl to cool.

recipes.title: Sauvignon Blanc Honey Vinaigrette
recipes.description: A bright, elegant vinaigrette with wine, lemon, and honey.

instructions.text: Whisk together shallot, lemon juice, zest, wine, salt, pepper, and honey.
Add olive oil in a slow stream, whisking until emulsified.

recipes.title: Pine Nut Gremolata
recipes.description: A crunchy Italian herb condiment with toasted pine nuts.

instructions.text: Place pine nuts, lemon zest, and basil in a small bowl. Add salt and pepper to taste. Stir in olive oil until all ingredients are well incorporated.

recipes.title: Pickled Red Pearl Onions
recipes.description: Tangy, spiced pickled onions for garnishing salads and plates.

instructions.text: Bring a large saucepan of salted water to a boil. Add pearl onions and blanch for 1 minute. Run under cold water to cool, then peel and transfer to a bowl.
Combine vinegars, water, sugar, salt, mustard seeds, peppercorns, coriander seeds, bay leaf, and red pepper flakes in a small saucepan and bring to a boil.
Strain the vinegar mixture over the onions and weigh them down with a small plate; all onions should be submerged. Set aside to cool.

recipes.title: Balsamic Vinaigrette
recipes.description: Classic balsamic dressing with shallots.

instructions.text: Place vinegar and minced shallot in a small bowl. Whisk in olive oil, taste for seasoning, and set aside.
If vinaigrette is too thick, add a teaspoon of water at a time until it reaches desired consistency.

recipes.title: Soy Ginger Vinaigrette
recipes.description: An Asian-inspired dressing with soy, ginger, and citrus.

instructions.text: Mince ginger and add to soy sauce, rice vinegar, and orange juice.
Put mustard in a bowl, whisk in the soy mixture and balsamic vinegar, and slowly stir in olive oil.

recipes.title: Brown Butter Vinaigrette
recipes.description: A rich, nutty vinaigrette with browned butter, citrus, and honey.

instructions.text: Melt the butter in a small saucepan over low heat until browned but not burnt, about 5 minutes. Set aside to cool slightly.
In a bowl, combine the lemon juice, orange juice, shallot, honey, and olive oil.
Whisk in the butter until emulsified. Season with salt and pepper.

tips: Watch the butter carefully—once it starts browning, it can burn in seconds. Remove from heat as soon as the milk solids turn golden.

recipes.title: Saffron Oil
recipes.description: Luxurious saffron-infused olive oil for drizzling on seafood dishes.

instructions.text: In a spice grinder or with a mortar and pestle, pulverize the saffron threads into a powder.
Pour the oil into a small jar and add the saffron powder.
Infuse for at least 30 minutes before using.

tips: This oil is optional but adds beautiful color and exotic flavor.

recipes.title: Garlic Crostini
recipes.description: Simple garlic-rubbed toasted bread for serving with soups and stews.

instructions.text: Preheat oven to 425°F.
Rub the baguette slices with the halved garlic clove on both sides and brush with olive oil.
Arrange on a small baking sheet and bake about 6 minutes, flipping halfway through, until golden brown.

recipes.title: Sesame Ginger Dressing
recipes.description: A savory-sweet Asian dressing with soy, ginger, and sesame.

instructions.text: Combine the soy sauce, rice vinegar, honey, and ginger, whisking to combine.
Whisk in the vegetable and sesame oils until well emulsified.
Fold in the sliced scallions.

recipes.title: Pink Grapefruit Dressing
recipes.description: A sweet-sour citrus vinaigrette with pink grapefruit and sherry vinegar.

instructions.text: In a small bowl, combine the grapefruit juice, shallot, honey, and sherry vinegar, whisking well.
Whisk in the olive oil in a slow, steady stream until emulsified.
Season with salt and pepper.

recipes.title: Parmesan Croutons
recipes.description: Crispy, cheesy homemade croutons baked with Parmesan.

instructions.text: Preheat the oven to 350°F.
Place the bread in a large bowl and toss with the olive oil. Add the Parmesan cheese and toss well to make sure that all of the bread is coated with the oil and the cheese.
Spread the bread on a parchment-lined sheet tray in a single layer and bake in the oven until golden brown, about 25-30 minutes.

recipes.title: Caesar Dressing
recipes.description: Creamy Caesar dressing with raw egg yolks, anchovy, and crème fraîche.

instructions.text: With an immersion blender, combine the mustard, crème fraîche, lemon juice, Parmesan cheese, egg yolks, anchovies, garlic, and salt and pepper and pulse until the ingredients are incorporated.
Scrape down the sides of the bowl with a rubber spatula. While the motor is running, add the oil in a slow and steady stream until the dressing begins to thicken and emulsify.
If it is too thick, add a few drops of water. Season with salt and pepper and more Parmesan cheese, anchovies, or lemon according to your taste.

tips: Uses raw egg yolks - ensure eggs are super-fresh, preferably from a local farm.

recipes.title: Yuzu Vinaigrette
recipes.description: A Japanese-inspired vinaigrette with tart yuzu citrus, soy sauce, and mustard.

instructions.text: In a small bowl, whisk together the yuzu juice, mustard, soy sauce, garlic, and lemon zest.
Add the oil in a slow, steady stream, whisking to emulsify.
Season to taste with salt and pepper.

tips: Yuzu juice can be found in Asian food stores. If unavailable, grapefruit juice may be substituted.

recipes.title: Pickled Radish, Fennel, and Carrot
recipes.description: Quick-pickled vegetables with Asian flavors - jalapeño, cilantro, and mustard seeds.

instructions.text: In a small saucepan, heat the vinegars, sugar, mustard seeds, and salt, mixing to dissolve. Bring to a simmer, then remove from the heat and cool slightly.
Combine the radishes, carrots, fennel, garlic clove, black peppercorns, and jalapeño in a bowl.
Pour the vinegar mixture over the vegetables, mixing to combine. Fold in the cilantro.
Transfer to a jar fitted with an airtight lid. Refrigerate overnight before using.

notes: Must be made one day ahead.

recipes.title: Lemon Vinaigrette
recipes.description: Simple lemon and Dijon vinaigrette.

instructions.text: In a small bowl, combine the lemon juice, Dijon mustard, and shallot.
Slowly whisk in olive oil. Season to taste with salt and pepper.

recipes.title: Candied Walnuts
recipes.description: Quick candied walnuts for topping salads.

instructions.text: Heat a medium nonstick skillet over medium heat.
Add walnuts, granulated sugar, and butter, stirring frequently until the butter melts and the nuts are well coated.
Transfer to a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and use a fork to separate the nuts right away.
Allow the coating to harden, 5-7 minutes.

tips: Separate the nuts immediately while still warm - they'll stick together as they cool.

recipes.title: Black Bean Mango Salsa
recipes.description: Fresh tropical salsa with black beans, mango, and cilantro.

instructions.text: In a medium bowl, combine the black beans, mango, red onion, yellow pepper, jalapeño, and garlic.
Add the vinegar, sugar, lime juice, and salt and pepper, and mix well.
Fold in the cilantro and allow to sit at room temperature so the flavors will develop.

tips: Let the salsa sit at room temperature for flavors to develop before serving.

recipes.title: Chili Vinaigrette
recipes.description: Spicy lime vinaigrette with cayenne and cumin.

instructions.text: Combine the lime juice, sherry vinegar, garlic, cayenne, cumin, and salt in a bowl.
Whisk in the oil until emulsified.
Stir in the parsley and set aside.

recipes.title: Gordon Ramsay's Kitchen Techniques & Tips
recipes.description: Essential kitchen techniques, knife cuts, and chef tips from Gordon Ramsay.

ingredients.prep_note: This is a techniques reference, not a recipe

instructions.text: Refer to the tips section for Gordon Ramsay's kitchen techniques and advice.

tips: COPPER BOWLS: If you love soufflés and meringues, consider investing in a copper bowl - it will enable you to whip voluptuous volume into your egg whites. Note that copper bowls are quite expensive and require that you clean and polish them before and after each use.

STEADYING BOWLS: If your mixing bowls don't have a nonskid base, try this trick to steady a bowl: Dampen a dish towel and wring out excess water, then, starting at one corner, roll up the towel to form a ring slightly larger than the base of your bowl; set your bowl inside its towel nest and proceed to mix and whisk securely.
BEST ALL-PURPOSE BOWL: If you're buying just one bowl type, stainless steel is your best bet.
TOASTING SPICES: Toast spices in a skillet just before using them to boost the flavor of your recipe.

BROWN BUTTER (Beurre Noisette): Brown butter—butter that's cooked until the milk fats separate from the butterfat and start to brown to a hazelnut color—is a classic French preparation. The trick to browning butter is to know when it's done, as it can go from browned to burnt in a matter of seconds. Once the butter melts, it foams a bit then subsides, and browned milk-solid specks form at the bottom of the pan. The specks continue to brown when the pan is removed from the heat, so to avoid turning your browned butter to burnt butter, take it off the heat as soon as the specks start to color.

TRUFFLES: There are more than seventy species of truffle, with the most prized being the black and white varieties. Their earthy, seductive, umami-rich flavor, unlike any other food on earth, makes them a cherished ingredient and among the most expensive foods in the world. French gastronome Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin called them the 'diamonds of the kitchen.'

TRUFFLE VARIETIES: Among the most sought-after truffles are the French black Périgord truffle and the white truffle of Alba from Piedmont, Italy. The white has a very short season, from fall to early winter. Black truffles are available in both summer and winter and typically are less expensive than the white.
TRUFFLE HUNTING: Truffles grow near trees, and specially trained pigs or dogs are employed to sniff them out from under the ground.

USING TRUFFLES: Truffles are typically grated or scraped on top of a dish (there's even a dedicated truffle slicer that can be used for the job), and a small amount is all you need to elevate a dish. They can transform a salad, take seared scallops to new heights, further elevate steak, are a natural with potatoes, pair perfectly with pasta and creamy sauces, and a little truffle atop an omelet is an upscale way to start your day.
TRUFFLE BUTTER: Making a compound butter by blending a little grated truffle into softened butter extends the essence of the truffle.
STORING TRUFFLES: Store fresh truffles for up to a couple of days in a jar of rice or a container filled with eggs to infuse them with the flavor and aroma of the truffles.

TRUFFLE OIL: Truffle oil, used in recipes throughout this book as a final flourish, is a way of adding truffle flavor to your dishes that's much lighter on the budget. Check your labels carefully, as many brands are made with artificial truffle flavoring; real truffle oil is olive oil infused with real truffles.
TRUFFLE SOURCES: Both truffles and truffle oil can be found in gourmet food stores. Online sources for truffles include Dartagnan.com, iGourmet.com, and Eataly.com.
MAKING PASTRY CRUST LIKE A PRO: Learning the basics of pastry making can be a valuable investment, as homemade pie crust is head-and-shoulders above anything you'll buy in a store.
PASTRY DOUGH STORAGE: Pastry dough is something you can make well in advance; wrapped tight in plastic, it keeps in the freezer for several months.

PASTRY DOUGH TYPES: Several recipes require making pastry dough—a standard pastry dough for apple pie, a sweet-tart dough enriched with sugar for passion fruit tart and lemon meringue tart, and a sablé Breton crust based in salted butter for raspberry crémeux tart.

FLAKY CRUST SECRET: Chef-quality pie crust starts with high-quality flour, and real butter is a must. Chilled butter, cut into chunks and rubbed into the dough or pulsed in a food processor, yields a flaky crust that skips the need for shortening.
notes: CUBE CUTS:
- CHOPPING: Cut food into squares about 1/2 inch in diameter; squares need not be perfectly uniform. Food may be coarsely chopped or chopped medium or fine.

- DICING: Cut food into even squares, more precise than chopping; important when even cooking is required. Large Dice: 3/4 inch square. Medium Dice (Macédoine): 1/2 inch square. Small Dice: 1/4 inch square. Brunoise: 1/8 inch square. Fine Brunoise: 1/16 inch square.
- MINCING: The smallest cut, smaller than dice or chop—basically as small as you can get the food. Often indicated for shallots and garlic.
STICK CUTS:
- BATONNET: 'Little stick'; 1/4 inch × 1/4 inch × 2 to 2-1/2 inches long (starting point for small dice)
- JULIENNE: 1/8 inch × 1/8 inch × 2 to 2-1/2 inches long (starting point for brunoise)
- FINE JULIENNE: 1/16 inch × 1/16 inch × 2 to 2-1/2 inches long (starting point for fine brunoise)
OTHER CUTS:
- DIAGONAL: Cut on an angle in varying sizes
- OBLIQUE OR ROLL CUT: Cut at an oblique angle, either by rolling the pieces or angling the knife
- PAYSANNE: 1/2 inch × 1/2 inch by 1/8 inch; a flat, square shape
- LOZENGE: 1/2 inch × 1/2 inch × 1/8 inch diamond shape
- FERMIÈRE: Cut lengthwise and sliced between 1/8 and 1/2 inch
- RONDELLE: Rounds cut between 1/8 and 1/2 inch
- TOURNÉ: An oblong cut that's 2 inches long with 7 faces

CHIFFONADE: The translation of chiffonade is 'rag,' so to chiffonade is to turn your food—typically herbs such as basil and green vegetables such as collards—into raglike strips. Strip the stems from your herb or vegetable, stack the leaves, roll them tightly, and slice crosswise into thin ribbons.
